justice: The street allocates substantial space to motor traffic with multiple wide vehicle lanes, while the pedestrian realm is limited to side sidewalks, indicating an uneven distribution of space across road users.
Sidewalks are visible on both sides of the road, which supports basic access for non-motorized users, but no dedicated bicycle lane or clearly protected cycling space is visible.
The sidewalks appear continuous and generally unobstructed by vendors or parked cars, which helps accessibility, but no curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossings are visible in the image.
safety: Lane markings are clear and the carriageway is wide, which helps organize vehicle movement and reduce immediate conflict between cars.
A planted median and roadside planting strips provide some separation between opposing traffic and the sidewalk edge, improving perceived safety for all users.
Safety for pedestrians is weakened because no zebra crossing, pedestrian signal, or refuge crossing point is visible on this long road segment.
A parked white car sits along the right curb, which may create some edge friction and visibility issues for people entering or crossing near the curb.
Streetlights are present, which supports nighttime safety, although the image does not show illumination performance.
livability: The corridor feels dominated by through-traffic function, with long asphalt lanes and sparse visible street activity, which limits everyday social vitality.
There are residential high-rise buildings on the right side, suggesting nearby habitation, but few active ground-floor uses or community-facing amenities are visible from the street.
Landscaped strips with shrubs and street trees add some environmental quality, yet there are no visible benches, kiosks, or gathering spaces that would support lingering or social use.
sustainability: Street trees and planted medians are visible, contributing some green infrastructure and modest ecological value along the corridor.
The presence of sidewalks on both sides supports non-motorized travel options, but no dedicated cycling infrastructure is visible, limiting support for low-carbon mode shift.
The road cross-section is heavily oriented toward private vehicle movement with broad asphalt surfaces, which generally increases impervious area and car dependence.
No visible permeable paving, bioswales, rain gardens, or other stormwater features can be identified from the image.
aesthetics: The boulevard has a relatively orderly composition, with aligned streetlights, lane markings, planted medians, and regularly spaced trees creating visual structure.
The roadway and curbs appear clean and well maintained, with smooth pavement and trimmed planting strips improving visual neatness.
Aesthetic quality is reduced by the gray sky, sparse winter-like tree canopy, and long expanses of dark asphalt, which make the scene feel somewhat monotonous.
The tall residential building provides an urban backdrop, but the street frontage lacks rich facade detail or active edge elements at eye level.
comfort: Thermal comfort appears limited because the street trees are relatively small and sparse, providing little visible shade over the sidewalks or roadway.
Physical comfort for walking is moderate at best: sidewalks appear paved and continuous, but no seating, shelters, or resting facilities are visible.
Psychological comfort is mixed because the road is wide and traffic-oriented, which can feel exposed for non-drivers even though traffic volume appears low in this moment.
The planted strips and setback from buildings soften the environment somewhat, but the broad open carriageway and lack of human-scale amenities reduce overall comfort.
walkability: Sidewalks are present on both sides and appear continuous, which supports basic pedestrian movement along the corridor.
Walkability is weakened by the very wide vehicular roadway and the absence of visible marked crosswalks or pedestrian crossing aids on this segment.
There are no visible benches, shade structures, storefronts, or active frontages to make walking more engaging or comfortable over distance.
The landscaped edge and trees improve the walking environment somewhat, but the corridor still reads primarily as a road for cars rather than a pedestrian-priority street.
